title: Research Bite #65: High Math Anxiety Is Associated With Lower Math Achievement Across 90 Countries Education
author: Tips for Teachers
summary: This research bite summarizes Brunner et al.'s 2025 individual participant data meta-analysis examining the relationship between math anxiety and math achievement across 2.5 million participants in 90 countries. The study found a consistent negative correlation of r = -.26, with math anxiety and low achievement forming a self-reinforcing cycle of avoidance and poor performance. Historical gender differences (females reporting stronger anxiety-achievement links) have largely disappeared in recent data. The relationship varies with GDP, individual achievement level, and major global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. For teachers, key implications include assessing both anxiety and achievement, adapting instruction to build confidence, fostering low-stakes environments that minimize evaluative pressure, and implementing targeted early interventions such as pre-test expressive writing. Caution is warranted because the study relies on low-stakes standardized tests and excludes early childhood settings.
points: Math anxiety and low achievement form a self-reinforcing cycle -- anxiety drives avoidance, avoidance reduces practice, reduced practice worsens performance -- and breaking the cycle requires targeted intervention before the pattern becomes entrenched.

A 'test-like' classroom environment that emphasizes constant success-failure evaluation amplifies the social comparison processes that trigger math anxiety; low-stakes formats reduce this pressure without sacrificing rigor.

Even light-touch interventions (having students write expressively about their math anxiety immediately before a test) have been shown to break the cycle -- teachers do not need resource-heavy programs to make a difference.

Teachers who assess both anxiety and achievement -- rather than relying solely on test scores -- catch the emotional and cognitive barriers that prevent learning from occurring, allowing for more targeted support.

The finding that gender differences in the anxiety-achievement link have largely vanished suggests that these disparities are responsive to instructional and cultural conditions, not fixed -- which strengthens the case for teacher-led intervention.
quotes: High math anxiety and lower math achievement share a reciprocal relationship that creates a self-reinforcing cycle of avoidance and poor performance. To break this cycle, implementing targeted interventions to reduce anxiety is essential for improving learning outcomes and keeping students engaged in STEM.

Our analysis revealed negative relationships between math anxiety and math achievement, observed to varying degrees across countries, grade levels, age groups, and genders; among individuals with low, average, and high math achievement; and across facets of math anxiety and math subdomains.

It is highly beneficial to avoid creating a strictly 'test-like' classroom environment that places a heavy emphasis on success and failure. Minimising constant evaluations by teachers or peers can reduce the evaluative pressures and unfavourable social comparison processes that are known to trigger and exacerbate math anxiety.

Consistent socioemotional and cognitive support from teachers can effectively mitigate the negative impacts of low math achievement on anxiety, and vice versa. Integrating socioemotional learning directly into the curriculum helps students better manage both the cognitive and affective demands of learning mathematics.

Teachers should utilise specific interventions, ideally starting at a young age, to break the self-reinforcing cycle of math avoidance and poor performance. These do not have to be resource-heavy; they can include low-cost, 'light touch' methods, such as having students engage in expressive writing about their math anxiety right before taking a test.

Because math anxiety impairs working memory, attention, and cognitive processing, teachers must look beyond academic test scores alone to fully address the emotional and cognitive barriers preventing students from learning.
